question: How are the primary flight controls normally powered?

options.text: Hydraulically, by systems A and B
Pneumatically, by bleed air actuators
Electrically, by the transfer buses
Manually, through cables and control tabs

explanation: Both hydraulic systems supply the primary controls, so the loss of one system does not reduce control authority.

question: What happens to the ailerons and elevators if both hydraulic systems fail?

options.text: They are powered by the standby hydraulic system
They revert to manual control through control tabs
They are driven electrically by backup actuators
They become locked in their last position

explanation: Manual reversion keeps the airplane controllable, although the forces required are considerably higher.

question: How does manual reversion work aerodynamically?

options.text: An electric backup motor assists the cable input
The pilot moves the surface directly through the cable run
The pilot moves a control tab, and the airflow over it moves the main surface
Spring cartridges hold the surface in the commanded position

explanation: Using the airflow to do the work is what makes it possible for a pilot to move a large surface without hydraulic assistance.

question: How is the rudder powered if both hydraulic systems A and B are lost?

options.text: By the standby hydraulic system
It is locked in the neutral position
It reverts to manual control through a tab
It is powered electrically

explanation: The rudder is the one primary control with a third hydraulic source, because directional control cannot be obtained manually at speed.

question: What do the flight control switches select besides ON and OFF?

options.text: The yaw damper
The elevator feel computer
The standby rudder system
The alternate flap drive

explanation: Selecting standby rudder brings in the third source without waiting for an automatic transfer.

question: What happens to the standby rudder if both system A and B pressure to the rudder is lost?

options.text: It is available only below 1000 ft
It must be selected manually on both flight control switches
It operates automatically
It provides partial rudder authority only after the flaps are extended

explanation: Automatic operation means the rudder is never left without a source during the time it takes the crew to diagnose the failure.

question: What does a flight control LOW PRESSURE light indicate?

options.text: Failure of the elevator feel computer
A low fluid quantity in the reservoir
Loss of the yaw damper
Low hydraulic pressure to the flight controls on that system

explanation: It reports the pressure actually reaching the controls, which can be lost even when the system still shows quantity.

question: What is the purpose of the aileron transfer mechanism?

options.text: It transfers roll control to the autopilot servos
It allows the control wheels to be separated if the aileron system jams
It connects the ailerons to the flight spoilers at low speed
It equalises the forces between the two control wheels in normal flight

explanation: With the system separated, one wheel continues to drive whatever remains free, so a jam does not remove all roll control.

question: What roll control remains available after the control wheels have been separated?

options.text: Ailerons on one side and flight spoilers on the other
Ailerons only, on the captain side
Rudder input through the yaw damper
Flight spoilers only

explanation: The two roll devices are driven from different wheels once separated, so the jam can only take one of them.

question: What is the equivalent provision if the elevator system jams?

options.text: The autopilot provides pitch control through its own servos
The stabiliser takes over pitch control automatically
The elevator reverts to manual control through the tabs
The control columns can be separated so each drives one elevator

explanation: Separating the columns means a jam on one side leaves the other elevator under control.

question: What is the function of the yaw damper?

options.text: It coordinates the rudder with aileron inputs during turns
It limits rudder deflection at high speed
It damps dutch roll oscillations by commanding small rudder movements
It trims the rudder for asymmetric thrust

explanation: A swept wing airplane is prone to a lightly damped lateral oscillation, and the damper suppresses it continuously.

question: Are yaw damper inputs felt through the rudder pedals?

options.text: Only above the flap retraction speed
Yes, the pedals move with every correction
Only when the autopilot is engaged
No, the pedals do not move with yaw damper inputs

explanation: Continuous pedal movement would be distracting and would mask the crew own inputs.

question: What is the purpose of reducing rudder system pressure in certain flight conditions?

options.text: To reduce hydraulic demand during the cruise
To prevent the yaw damper from saturating
To allow the standby system to be tested in flight
To limit rudder authority where full deflection is not needed and could overstress the fin

explanation: Full rudder authority is needed at low speed but becomes excessive at higher speeds. Verify the exact logic against your operator FCOM.

question: How is pitch trim achieved?

options.text: By deflecting a trim tab on the elevator
By biasing the elevator feel computer
By repositioning the elevator neutral point electrically
By moving the horizontal stabiliser

explanation: Moving the whole stabiliser gives a large trim range with very little drag penalty.

question: By which means can the stabiliser be trimmed?

options.text: Manually only
Electrically from the control wheel switches, by the autopilot, or manually with the trim wheels
Electrically only
By the autopilot only, with manual reversion available on the ground

explanation: Three independent paths mean a trim failure in one does not leave the airplane out of trim.

question: What is the effect of moving the control column opposite to the direction of stabiliser trim movement?

options.text: Electric trim in that direction is stopped
The trim rate is reduced by half
The autopilot disengages
The manual trim wheels are disconnected

explanation: Column movement against a runaway is the instinctive reaction, so it is used to cut the electric trim automatically.

question: What do the stabiliser trim cutout switches do?

options.text: They disconnect the manual trim wheels
They isolate the elevator feel computer
They remove electric power from the stabiliser trim
They lock the stabiliser in its current position mechanically

explanation: Cutting the power stops any uncommanded electric trim, leaving the manual wheels as the means of trimming.

question: What remains available after the stabiliser trim cutout switches have been used?

options.text: No trim capability at all
Autopilot trim only
Manual trim using the trim wheels
Electric trim at a reduced rate

explanation: The mechanical path is independent of the electrical system, which is why it survives the cutout.

question: How is stabiliser position displayed to the crew?

options.text: Only by the position of the trim wheel handle
In units on the trim indicator beside the trim wheels
As a percentage on the flight display
As an angle in degrees on the overhead panel

explanation: The indicator is beside the wheels so the setting and its movement are seen together.

question: Why is the movement of the trim wheels significant to the crew?

options.text: Their rotation drives the autopilot pitch servo
Their movement and sound provide a direct indication that trim is running
They show the position of the elevator feel computer
They indicate the hydraulic pressure available to the stabiliser

explanation: An uncommanded trim runaway is recognised first by the wheels turning when nobody has commanded it.

question: What is the purpose of the elevator feel computer?

options.text: It provides artificial feel to the rudder pedals
It varies the control column force according to airspeed and stabiliser position
It limits elevator deflection at low speed
It compensates for Mach tuck at high speed

explanation: Without artificial feel, a hydraulically powered control would give the pilot no sense of how much load is being applied.

question: What does a FEEL DIFF PRESS light indicate?

options.text: A failure of the stabiliser trim system
An asymmetry between the two elevators
A difference in pressure between hydraulic systems A and B
A difference between the pressures supplied to the elevator feel system

explanation: The system is duplicated, and a disagreement means one half may not be providing the correct feel.

question: What is the purpose of the Mach trim system?

options.text: It trims the rudder for asymmetric thrust at high speed
It limits the maximum Mach number that can be selected
It adjusts the elevator feel forces at low speed
It compensates for the nose down tendency that develops at high Mach number

explanation: The rearward movement of the centre of pressure at high Mach produces a pitch down that must be trimmed out automatically.

question: What does a MACH TRIM FAIL light mean for the crew?

options.text: The stabiliser trim must be cut out
A speed restriction may apply because the compensation is no longer available
The autopilot must be disengaged immediately
The airplane must descend below 10000 ft

explanation: Without the compensation the airplane is limited to speeds where the effect remains manageable.

question: What is the purpose of the speed trim system?

options.text: It prevents the stabiliser from exceeding the takeoff trim range
It trims the airplane automatically during the approach
It improves speed stability by trimming the stabiliser at low speed and high thrust
It maintains the selected airspeed by adjusting the thrust

explanation: At light weight, aft centre of gravity and high thrust the airplane is less speed stable, and the system restores that stability.

question: When does the speed trim system operate?

options.text: Whenever the autopilot is engaged
Only above the flap retraction altitude
With the autopilot not engaged, in the conditions for which it is designed
Only with the flaps fully retracted

explanation: It exists to help the pilot flying manually, so it is not needed when the autopilot is trimming the airplane.

question: What is the relationship between the flight spoilers and the control wheel?

options.text: They are driven only by the autopilot roll channel
They deploy symmetrically with wheel movement
They are unaffected by the control wheel
They rise on the down going wing to assist roll control

explanation: Spoiler assistance increases roll rate, which matters most at low speed where aileron effectiveness is reduced.

question: Which spoiler panels operate only on the ground?

options.text: The flight spoilers
The ground spoilers
All spoiler panels operate in flight and on the ground
The inboard flight spoilers only

explanation: Their deflection is too large for flight use, and they exist to destroy lift and put weight on the wheels after touchdown.

question: What determines the number of spoiler panels on each wing?

options.text: Whether blended winglets are fitted
The maximum certificated takeoff weight
The autobrake system installed
The build and configuration of that airplane

explanation: Panel counts differ between variants and builds. Verify the arrangement on your fleet against your operator FCOM.

question: What are the positions of the speedbrake lever?

options.text: DOWN, HALF and FULL
OFF, FLIGHT and GROUND
DOWN, ARMED, FLIGHT DETENT and UP
RETRACT, ARM and EXTEND

explanation: Each position corresponds to a different combination of flight and ground spoiler operation.

question: What does the ARMED position achieve?

options.text: Deployment of the flight spoilers to the flight detent
Automatic speedbrake deployment on landing
Extension of the ground spoilers before touchdown
Automatic retraction of the speedbrakes at a preset speed

explanation: Automatic deployment at touchdown puts the spoilers up immediately, which is when they are most valuable for braking.

question: What normally triggers the automatic speedbrake deployment after landing?

options.text: The autobrake system reaching its selected deceleration
Nose wheel contact with the runway
Selection of reverse thrust
Wheel spin up or the main gear compressing, with the thrust levers at idle

explanation: The logic confirms the airplane is actually on the ground before deploying a device that destroys lift.

question: What is the purpose of the flight detent?

options.text: It limits spoiler deflection to the maximum permitted in flight
It holds the lever until wheel spin up occurs
It arms the ground spoilers for landing
It selects the spoilers for roll assistance only

explanation: A stop in the lever travel prevents the pilot from selecting a deflection that is only appropriate on the ground.

question: What does the SPEED BRAKE DO NOT ARM light indicate?

options.text: A fault in the automatic speedbrake system
That the speedbrakes are extended in flight
That the ground spoilers have failed to retract
That the lever is in the armed position

explanation: It tells the crew that the automatic function cannot be relied on, so manual deployment must be planned.

question: Why do the speedbrakes not deploy the ground spoilers in flight?

options.text: Because the autobrake system inhibits them
Because the lever cannot be moved beyond the flight detent on the ground
Because they are powered only by the standby hydraulic system
Because their deflection would produce an unacceptable loss of lift

explanation: The devices are designed to destroy lift completely, which is useful after touchdown and dangerous in the air.

question: What is the role of the automatic speedbrake during a rejected takeoff?

options.text: The spoilers deploy only if the autobrakes are selected to maximum
The spoilers remain stowed until reverse thrust is selected
The spoilers are inhibited below V1
The spoilers deploy automatically to place weight on the wheels

explanation: Weight on the wheels is what makes the brakes effective, so the spoilers contribute directly to the stopping distance.

question: Which hydraulic system normally drives the trailing edge flaps?

options.text: System A
Both A and B simultaneously
The standby system
System B

explanation: A single system drives them, with an alternate electric drive available if that system is lost.

question: Which hydraulic system normally drives the leading edge devices?

options.text: The standby system
System B
System A
The alternate electric drive

explanation: Splitting the leading and trailing edge drives between the two systems prevents a single failure from taking all the high lift devices.

question: What are the selectable flap positions?
explanation: The range covers everything from a small takeoff setting to a full landing setting for short runways.

question: What happens when the first flap detents are selected?

options.text: The leading edge devices extend before any significant trailing edge movement
The leading edge devices remain retracted until flap 5
Only the trailing edge flaps extend
Both leading and trailing edge devices extend together

explanation: Extending the leading edge first protects the wing at increasing angles of attack as the airplane slows.

question: What are the two types of leading edge device fitted?

options.text: Slats inboard and Krueger flaps outboard
Krueger flaps inboard and slats outboard
Slats across the whole leading edge
Krueger flaps across the whole leading edge

explanation: The inboard and outboard sections of the wing have different requirements, so different devices are used.

question: What is indicated by the leading edge devices annunciator panel?

options.text: The transit and extended position of each leading edge device
The selected flap lever position
The asymmetry between the left and right devices only
The hydraulic pressure available to the leading edge system

explanation: Individual indications are what allow an asymmetry or a failed panel to be identified rather than just suspected.

question: What is the purpose of flap load relief?

options.text: It retracts the flaps from the full landing setting if the placard speed is exceeded
It reduces the flap extension rate at high speed
It limits the flap lever to an intermediate setting above a given weight
It prevents flap extension above the maximum altitude

explanation: The system protects the structure automatically and then restores the setting once the speed has been reduced.

question: What happens after flap load relief has operated and the speed is reduced?

options.text: The flap lever must be cycled to restore the setting
The alternate flap system must be used to re-extend them
The flaps re-extend to the selected position automatically
The flaps remain at the reduced setting until reselected

explanation: The automatic restoration means the crew retains the landing configuration they selected once the speed is back within limits.

question: How are the trailing edge flaps extended if the normal hydraulic drive fails?

options.text: Electrically, using the alternate flap system
By the standby hydraulic system
They cannot be extended and a flapless landing is required
By gravity with an unlocking handle

explanation: An electric drive is independent of the hydraulic failure that caused the problem.

question: How are the leading edge devices extended when the alternate system is used?

options.text: By the alternate electric drive
By the remaining main hydraulic system
By the standby hydraulic system
By aerodynamic load once the trailing edge flaps extend

explanation: The standby system is the third hydraulic source, and it is used here as well as for the rudder.

question: What is the most important operational characteristic of an alternate leading edge extension?

options.text: It extends the devices only to the intermediate position
It requires the flaps to be at the full landing setting first
It cannot be reversed, so the devices cannot be retracted afterwards
It is slower but otherwise identical to normal operation

explanation: Because a go around cannot be flown in a clean configuration afterwards, the decision to use it is made with the landing committed.

question: What is the purpose of the autoslat function?

options.text: It drives the slats to the full extend position as the airplane approaches a stall
It prevents slat extension above the placard speed
It retracts the slats automatically at high speed
It extends the slats automatically when the flap lever is moved

explanation: Additional leading edge camber at high angle of attack improves the stall margin at the moment it is most needed.

question: What is the purpose of the stick shaker?

options.text: It warns of an asymmetric flap condition
It warns the crew of an approaching stall
It indicates a flight control hydraulic failure
It signals an autopilot disconnect

explanation: A tactile warning reaches the pilot through the hands even when attention is elsewhere.

question: Is a stick pusher fitted to this airplane?

options.text: Yes, it is armed automatically below 1000 ft
Yes, it operates after the stick shaker
Yes, but only with the flaps retracted
No, stall protection is provided by warning and increased control forces

explanation: Recovery depends on the pilot responding to the warning, which is why recognition and the correct technique are trained so heavily.

question: What is the purpose of the elevator feel shift function?

options.text: It softens the feel forces during the flare
It reduces column force during manual reversion
It increases column force at high angle of attack to discourage further back pressure
It compensates for stabiliser position changes

explanation: Making the airplane feel heavy as the stall is approached adds a second, physical layer to the stall warning.

question: Which control surface provides primary directional control?

options.text: The rudder
The ailerons
The flight spoilers
The stabiliser

explanation: It is also the surface that handles the asymmetry after an engine failure, which is why it has three hydraulic sources.

question: Why does the rudder have a third hydraulic source when the ailerons and elevators do not?

options.text: Because manual reversion is not certified for the rudder
Because the yaw damper requires a dedicated supply
Because directional control cannot be maintained manually at high speed with asymmetric thrust
Because the rudder is the largest control surface

explanation: The consequence of losing rudder power in an asymmetric condition is far more immediate than losing power to the other surfaces.

question: What is the handling consequence of manual reversion?

options.text: Roll control is lost entirely
Pitch control is available only through the stabiliser
Control response is unchanged but trim is unavailable
Control forces are considerably higher and response is slower

explanation: Flying without hydraulic assistance is physically demanding, and the technique relies on trimming and on anticipating control inputs.

question: What is the effect of losing hydraulic system A alone on the flight controls?

options.text: Manual reversion occurs immediately
The controls remain fully powered by system B
The ailerons are lost and roll control depends on the spoilers
The rudder transfers to the standby system automatically

explanation: The dual supply to each primary surface is exactly what makes a single system loss manageable.

question: Why is the loss of one hydraulic system nevertheless significant for the flight controls?

options.text: Because the yaw damper is lost with either system
Because the primary controls revert to manual
Because the high lift devices and some spoiler panels depend on the individual systems
Because the stabiliser trim becomes unavailable

explanation: The primary surfaces are unaffected, but the configuration changing systems are split between A and B.

question: What is the purpose of the flap position indicator?

options.text: It shows the actual position of the trailing edge flaps
It shows the difference between the left and right flaps
It shows the leading edge device positions
It shows the position selected on the flap lever only

explanation: Confirming the surfaces have reached the selected position is what turns a selection into a verified configuration.

question: What is the danger of an asymmetric flap or slat condition?

options.text: Loss of the stall warning system
An uncommanded yaw towards the higher flap setting
A rolling moment that may exceed the available roll control
An immediate loss of pitch control

explanation: Lift differs between the wings, and if the asymmetry is large enough the ailerons and spoilers cannot balance it.

question: How is an asymmetry normally prevented from developing?

options.text: By mechanically linking the left and right surfaces
By limiting the rate of flap extension
By restricting flap selection to one detent at a time
By a protection system that stops flap or slat movement when an asymmetry is sensed

explanation: Stopping the drive at the first sign of a mismatch limits the asymmetry to a size the controls can handle.

question: What is the purpose of the takeoff trim setting range?

options.text: It arms the speed trim system
It limits the trim available after takeoff
It sets the elevator feel forces for the takeoff
It ensures the stabiliser is set within the range appropriate for the loaded centre of gravity

explanation: A stabiliser set outside the range produces either an unmanageable rotation or an unexpected pitch up.

question: Why is the takeoff configuration warning related to the flight control systems?

options.text: Because it checks the flap and stabiliser settings before takeoff
Because it verifies the yaw damper is engaged
Because it confirms the speedbrake lever is armed
Because it monitors the hydraulic pressure to the controls

explanation: The warning exists because attempting a takeoff with the wrong configuration has repeatedly proved fatal.

question: Why are the flight and ground spoilers powered from different hydraulic sources across the panels?

options.text: To allow the autobrake system to control them independently
So that a single hydraulic failure leaves some spoiler capability available
Because the ground spoilers require higher pressure
To balance the hydraulic demand between the systems

explanation: Distributing the panels means a system failure degrades the spoiler function rather than removing it.

question: What is the effect of extending the speedbrakes in flight?

options.text: The airplane slows without any change in descent rate
Lift is reduced and drag is increased, producing a higher rate of descent
Drag is increased with no change in lift
Lift is increased and the airplane pitches down

explanation: Because they spoil lift as well as adding drag, their use is limited in the approach configuration.

question: Why is a stabiliser trim runaway treated as a memory item?

options.text: Because it disables the autopilot permanently
Because an unchecked runaway can produce forces the crew cannot overcome
Because the electrical system will be damaged
Because it causes an immediate loss of hydraulic pressure

explanation: The stabiliser is powerful enough to exceed elevator authority, so the time available to react is short.

question: What is the relationship between stabiliser position and elevator authority?

options.text: A large out of trim stabiliser can overcome the available elevator authority
The stabiliser only affects trim forces, not authority
The elevator can always override the stabiliser
They are independent of each other

explanation: The stabiliser is the larger surface with the longer moment arm, which is why an out of trim condition must not be allowed to develop.

question: What is the purpose of the flight control system test before flight?

options.text: To exercise the autopilot servos
To confirm full and free movement of the controls in the correct sense
To reset the flight control computers
To verify the hydraulic pump output pressure

explanation: A restriction or a reversed connection can only be found by moving the controls and observing the result before flight.

question: Why are the primary flight controls checked for correct sense as well as free movement?

options.text: Because the hydraulic pressure differs in each direction
Because a control connected in reverse would still move freely
Because the autopilot requires a directional reference
Because the feel forces differ in each direction

explanation: Free movement alone proves nothing about which way the surface goes, and the history of accidents includes reversed connections.

question: Why is high lift device selection restricted by placard speeds?

options.text: Because the extended surfaces and their mechanisms cannot withstand the loads at higher speeds
Because the stall warning system is calibrated for specific speeds
Because the autopilot cannot compensate for the trim change
Because the hydraulic drives cannot move them against the airflow

explanation: The devices are large, lightly built structures optimised for low speed, and exceeding their limit speeds damages them.
